hello.native: สวัสดีเน้อ/เจ้า
hello.note: Men close with noe, women with jao — Kam Mueang's own particles in place of standard Thai's khrap/kha. Written in Thai script here, the everyday way it's typed today, though the old Lanna Tai Tham script is the traditional one.

good_morning.native: สวัสดีตอนเจ้าเน้อ/เจ้า
good_morning.note: 'Dton-jao' (morning) happens to look just like the jao particle in Thai script; likely reflects the dialect's own ch-to-j sound shift.

good_evening.native: สวัสดีตอนแลงเน้อ/เจ้า
good_evening.note: Laeng is the north's own word for evening, a different root from standard Thai yen.

goodbye.native: ไปละเน้อ/เจ้า
goodbye.note: Literally 'I'm off now'; the everyday way to part.

how_are_you.native: สบายดีบ่เน้อ/เจ้า
how_are_you.note: Sa-bai dee ('well') plus bor, the north's own yes/no question particle, mirroring standard Thai's sabai dee mai. The 'you' pronoun is dropped, normal for direct address; an earlier draft used peun here, but Wikipedia's Lanna-language grammar table glosses peun (เปิ้น) as third-person 'he/she', not 'you', so it was removed as an error.

thank_you.native: ขอบใจ๋เน้อ
thank_you.note: Sources give this same form for both men and women, unlike most other phrases here.

youre_welcome.native: ยินดีเน้อ/เจ้า
youre_welcome.note: Built on the shared Thai root yin-dee ('glad, pleased', per Wiktionary) plus the north's own khap/jao particle (confirmed on Wikipedia's Lanna-language page). Checked several dictionaries and phrase blogs; none give a distinct Kam Mueang word for this reply, so the standard-Thai reply-to-thanks pattern (as in the Thai entry's yin-dee khrap/kha) is kept rather than reusing bor-pen-yang, which would collide with no_problem below.

no_problem.native: บ่เป็นหยังเน้อ/เจ้า
no_problem.note: The north's own 'no worries', mirroring standard Thai mai pen rai; a Chiang Mai massage-shop phrase blog gives bor pen yang itself as 'no worries/it's okay'.

please.note: Shared with standard Thai; no distinct Kam Mueang word is documented, and politeness is carried by noe/jao.

excuse_me.note: An old-school Lanna phrase rooted in the Buddhist custom of asking pardon (sumaa); still heard from elders.

sorry.note: One phrase covers both 'excuse me' and 'sorry', as in standard Thai.

yes.note: Wikipedia's Lanna-language grammar page lists khap and jao as the two polite final particles, khap for males and jao for females; jao is also glossed on Wiktionary as a female particle for affirmation/assent. Neither source glosses khap directly as a standalone 'yes', so treat that half as inferred by symmetry.

no.native: บ่เน้อ/เจ้า
no.note: Bor is the north's own word for 'not/no', replacing standard Thai mai.

of_course.native: แน่นอนเน้อ/เจ้า
of_course.note: Shared Thai root nae-non ('surely, certainly', per Wiktionary) plus the northern particle; checked dictionaries and phrase blogs and found no distinct Kam Mueang phrase, so this follows the same pattern as the Thai entry's nae-non khrap/kha.

amazing.note: Muan means fun/wonderful in Kam Mueang; doubling it with taetae ('really, truly') gives the emphasis.

delicious.native: ลำเน้อ/เจ้า
delicious.note: Lam is the north's own word for delicious, replacing standard Thai aroi.

slang.note: Doubling down for 'truly delicious'; the north's favorite food compliment, warm and used with anyone.

cheers.native: ชนแก้วเน้อ/เจ้า
cheers.note: No distinct Kam Mueang toast is attested; this is the shared Thai 'clink glasses' phrase with the northern particle.
